analysis.one_liner: Cuts off drug patent terms once a first patent expires, limiting multiple overlapping patents.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a vote or a single cosponsor, leaving brand-name drug makers' patent practices unchanged.
analysis.plain_summary: Drug makers often obtain many patents on one drug—small changes, new uses, new forms—so that even after the main patent ends, later patents keep cheaper generic or biosimilar copies off the market for years. This bill would presume that a patent holder gives up (disclaims) patent term on later patents after the first one expires, unless the maker proves the later patents cover genuinely different inventions. It would also require the patent office to review whether its exam procedures are improperly granting overlapping drug patents.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who pay high prices for brand-name drugs would benefit if overlapping patents stopped blocking cheaper generic and biosimilar versions. Generic and biosimilar manufacturers would gain clearer access to the market once the first patent expires.

how_it_helps.text: The bill presumes that drug patents expire when the first patent on the drug expires, unless the maker proves the later patents cover patentably distinct inventions, which shortens the effective monopoly period created by multiple overlapping patents [S2].

It requires the Director of the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office to review examination procedures and recommend ways to reduce the improper issuance of patents that improperly extend a drug's exclusivity [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies would bear the cost: overlapping patents could no longer be used to extend market exclusivity, reducing the years of monopoly pricing revenue on drugs with patent thickets.

drawbacks.text: The presumption is not absolute: a patentee who demonstrates by a preponderance of the evidence that later patents cover patentably distinct inventions keeps full patent term, so the bill only stops patents that are not genuinely distinct [S2].
The review of patent examination procedures is only a study and report to the House Judiciary Committee, with no requirement that the patent office change its practices [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit—cheaper generic and biosimilar competition reaching patients sooner—is real but indirect and hard to predict; the bill keeps a fair escape hatch for genuinely distinct inventions, so legitimate drug patents are not harmed. The USPTO study adds scrutiny but no enforcement teeth. On balance a modest, targeted change against patent thickets, with the cost falling on brand-name manufacturers' extended monopoly revenue.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Pat Ryan introduced the bill on November 15, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day [S1].
The referral to Judiciary was the bill's only action; no cosponsors signed on, and no further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical companies are better off: the overlapping-patent practices the bill targeted remain in place, and no competing proposal advanced.

for.name: Rep. Pat Ryan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on November 15, 2023; it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S1].

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jim Jordan (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral—no hearing, no markup, no floor consideration [S4].

sides.party_line_note: The sole sponsor was a House Democrat, the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, and the Republican-chared Judiciary Committee never acted on it [S3].

industries.note: The bill would prevent overlapping patents from extending a drug's market exclusivity past the first patent's expiration, cutting years of monopoly pricing revenue. Its interest in blocking or ignoring the bill runs against patients who pay higher prices for longer.
Shorter effective exclusivity means generic and biosimilar copies could reach the market sooner once the first patent expires. Their interest runs alongside patients seeking lower drug prices.
